'''''Lotus creticus''''' is a species of [[Perennial plant|perennial herb]] of the family [[Fabaceae]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=creta trefoil - Encyclopedia of Life|url=https://eol.org/pages/702890|access-date=2021-09-02|website=eol.org}}</ref> found in tropical Africa.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Lotus creticus in Global Plants on JSTOR|url=https://plants.jstor.org/compilation/Lotus.creticus|access-date=2021-09-04|website=plants.jstor.org}}</ref> It is symbiosis-competent and engages in nitrogen-fixing symbiotic interactions with species of the Ensifer genus[3][3]. It comprises three varieties found in the Mediterranean. There is some controversy as to whether each subgroup could be considered the same species but are classically described as being subgroups.<ref name=":4" /> Varieties consist of the most commonly cited silky-hairy var. ''creticus'', which is widely distributed in its western part of the coast; the non-silky var. glabrescens, which has a western Mediterranean distribution; and the eastern Mediterranean var. collinus, which is also not silky and can be described by long [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] and peduncles.<ref name=":4" />

== Morphology ==
''Lotus creticus'' has been described as a perennial herb of 1–2F with diffuse copiously-branched densely grey-silky Appearance.<ref name=":1" /> Leaflets are fleshy and oblanceolate-cuneate. Flowers are in umbels with 4–8 on axillary peduncles.<ref name=":1" /> Pedicels are described as short and bracts as a compound, equalling or shorter than the calyx.<ref name=":1" /> Flowers are corolla yellow and twice the calyx with linear pods linear of 12–18 lines long, turgid with 9–15-seeds per pod.<ref name=":0" />

== Symbiosis == 
''Lotus creticus'' has been found to engage in nitrogen-fixing symbiosis with ''[[Ensifer numidicus]].''<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Merabet |first1=C. |last2=Martens |first2=M. |last3=Mahdhi |first3=M. |last4=Zakhia |first4=F. |last5=Sy |first5=A. |last6=Le Roux |first6=C. |last7=Domergue |first7=O. |last8=Coopman |first8=R. |last9=Bekki |first9=A. |last10=Mars |first10=M. |last11=Willems |first11=A. |date=March 2010 |title=Multilocus sequence analysis of root nodule isolates from Lotus arabicus (Senegal), Lotus creticus, Argyrolobium uniflorum and Medicago sativa (Tunisia) and description of Ensifer numidicus sp. nov. and Ensifer garamanticus sp. nov |journal=International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Microbiology |volume=60 |issue=Pt 3 |pages=664–674 |doi=10.1099/ijs.0.012088-0 |issn=1466-5026 |pmid=19656922 |bibcode=2010IJSEM..60..664M |hdl-access=free |hdl=1854/LU-936490}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
''Lotus creticus'' is native to the Spanish Mediterranean coast.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|date=2004-09-10|title=Effects of water stress and night temperature preconditioning on water relations and morphological and anatomical changes of Lotus creticus plants|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304423804000068|journal=Scientia Horticulturae|language=en|volume=101|issue=3|pages=333–342|doi=10.1016/j.scienta.2003.11.007|issn=0304-4238|last1=Bañon |first1=S. |last2=Fernandez |first2=J.A |last3=Franco |first3=J.A |last4=Torrecillas |first4=A. |last5=Alarcón |first5=J.J |last6=Sánchez-Blanco |first6=M.J |bibcode=2004ScHor.101..333B |url-access=subscription }}</ref> It can be found in a wide range of habitats ranging from sandy to heavy saline soils and from sea level to high altitudes.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Heyn|first1=C. C.|last2=Herrnstadt|first2=I.|date=1967|title=The Lotus creticus Group|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4108523|journal=Kew Bulletin|volume=21|issue=2|pages=299–309|doi=10.2307/4108523|jstor=4108523 |bibcode=1967KewBu..21..299H |issn=0075-5974|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Importance ==
''Lotus creticus'' is used in agriculture as an alternative to traditional covering plants as they experience rapid growth, have higher yields than traditional alternatives, and are considered drought-resistant.<ref name=":3" />  ''L. creticus'' is also considered an important candidate for revegetation programs in Europe.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last1=Escaray|first1=F. J.|last2=Rosique|first2=F. J. C.|last3=Scambato|first3=A. A.|last4=Bilenca|first4=D.|last5=Carrasco|first5=P.|last6=Matarredona|first6=A. V.|last7=Ruiz|first7=O. A.|last8=Menéndez|first8=A. B.|date=2010|title=Evaluation of a technical revegetation action performed on foredunes at Devesa de la Albufera, Valencia, Spain|journal=Land Degradation & Development|language=en|volume=21|issue=3|pages=239–247|doi=10.1002/ldr.970|doi-access=free |bibcode=2010LDeDe..21..239E |s2cid=140579330 |issn=1099-145X}}</ref> It is a pioneer plant and can rapidly advance in poor soils. In studies comparing similar species in bioremediation, ''L. creticus'' showed the highest levels of dominance at the initial and oldest stages of the revegetation.<ref name=":5" />
